one_liner: LD_PRELOAD heap profiler for Linux recording every allocation with full backtraces, positioned as a cheaper heaptrack/massif alternative.
what_it_does: Bytehound is a Rust cdylib (libbytehound.so) that you LD_PRELOAD into a native program; it interposes malloc/calloc/realloc/memalign/free (and jemalloc's prefixed _rjem_* entry points), records every allocation and deallocation with a stack trace, and writes a .dat file. A separate bytehound CLI serves a web GUI, runs Rhai scripts over the data, strips short-lived allocations, and exports JSON, heaptrack format or flamegraphs. Profiling can be toggled with SIGUSR1/SIGUSR2 and streamed over TCP to another machine.
how_it_is_fast: The speed claim rests on custom unwinding from koute's not-perf crates (nwind): per-thread and global backtrace caches deduplicate stacks (16384 and 327680 entries by default), and a 'shadow stack' mode, on by default, is described as a more intrusive, faster unwinding algorithm; turning it off 'will on average significantly slow down unwinding'. Allocations are still served by the real glibc (or jemalloc) allocator with a small tracking id appended to each block, and the profiler's own memory comes from a vendored mimalloc. The 0.10.0 release notes say CPU overhead on allocation-heavy multithreaded programs dropped by up to about 80%, but no comparison against heaptrack or Valgrind is published.
when_to_use: Finding leaks, peak-memory culprits, temporary-allocation churn or fragmentation in C, C++ or Rust programs on Linux without recompiling
Long-running services, using MEMORY_PROFILER_CULL_TEMPORARY_ALLOCATIONS to keep only allocations that live longer than a threshold (default 10 s)
Profiling on memory-constrained targets (AMD64, ARM, AArch64, MIPS64) by streaming data to another machine
Rust programs using the jemallocator crate on AMD64, which heaptrack-style malloc hooks miss
When you want scriptable analysis (Rhai) or want to export into the heaptrack GUI
when_not_to_use: If you need a measured overhead guarantee: the project publishes no numbers against heaptrack, massif or DHAT
macOS, Windows or any non-Linux target

When you need a maintained tool: last commit 2023-07-28, 44 open issues including segfaults under LD_PRELOAD (#93), aarch64 unwind-table failures (#114) and infinite recursion when glibc's __tls_get_addr calls malloc (#131, 2025)
Programs that fork without exec, or that rely heavily on longjmp/setjmp: child tracking after fork is a reported problem (#80) and longjmp is only partially supported
Very long full-detail captures: data files can exceed RAM at analysis time and the strip subcommand itself can run out of memory (#113)

integration.dependencies: Building needs GCC, Rust nightly (rust-toolchain pins nightly-2022-10-13; README says only 1.62 or newer) and Yarn for the web GUI; runtime needs only LD_PRELOAD
integration.platforms: Linux on AMD64, ARM, AArch64, MIPS64 (MIPS64 needs an out-of-tree perf_event_open kernel patch); jemalloc profiling AMD64-only
integration.thread_safety: Profiles multithreaded programs with per-thread unwind contexts and backtrace caches
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same LD_PRELOAD workflow as heaptrack and can export heaptrack files, but its own .dat format, CLI and GUI differ from massif/DHAT

gotchas: Each allocation is enlarged by an internal tracking id stored at the end of the usable block, so the profiled program's memory layout and malloc_usable_size results differ from an unprofiled run.

The fast shadow-stack unwinder is intrusive; past releases fixed crashes from calling backtrace and from exceptions under it, and it can be disabled with MEMORY_PROFILER_USE_SHADOW_STACK=0 at a large unwinding cost.
By default it embeds the program binary and all loaded libraries into the output file (MEMORY_PROFILER_WRITE_BINARIES_TO_OUTPUT=1), which inflates files and can leak binaries if the .dat is shared.
SIGUSR1 and SIGUSR2 handlers are installed by default and will collide with programs that use those signals.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over heaptrack when you need jemalloc-aware profiling, temporary-allocation culling for multi-day runs, remote streaming or scriptable analysis; pick heaptrack (maintained by KDE) or memtrail when you want an actively maintained tool, and tracing_malloc if you need a published wall-time comparison against Valgrind.
verified_claims_summary: No measurement exists: the README only says its custom unwinding makes it 'a lot cheaper than other similar tools, potentially up to orders of magnitude faster in some cases', without naming a baseline, hardware or workload. The heaptrack/Valgrind comparison comes from the author's Hacker News comments (search snippets only), and issue #55 asking for a heaptrack comparison has no answer.
status_note: Abandoned since 2023-07-28 (last release 0.11.0) but dual Apache-2.0/MIT licensed with 4.8k stars; building needs the pinned 2022 nightly Rust toolchain.
